interest_reason: Reinvesting resources into generators in a strategy or idle game is literally interest earning interest.
concept_explanation: Compound interest means interest is calculated on the original amount plus all the interest already earned. Each period the balance is multiplied by (1 + r), so after t periods the amount is A = P(1 + r)^t. Growth is slow at first and then speeds up, because each period's interest is larger than the last. Simple interest pays only on the original principal, so it grows by the same fixed amount every period.
analogy_narrative: You start a strategy game with 1,000 gold. Every 100 gold buys a mine that produces 10 gold per round, so your gold earns 10% each round. Option one: bank the gold the mines make. Option two: spend it immediately on more mines. In the first rounds the two look almost the same. But in option two each round's new gold builds new mines, which produce more gold, which builds more mines. By round ten the reinvesting player has about 2,594 gold and the banking player has 2,000, and the gap keeps widening every round after that.

Linear (simple) versus exponential (compound): the gap widens every period.

analogy_limits: Game formulas are guaranteed. Real investment returns go up and down, and only savings accounts or fixed deposits come close to a fixed rate.
Real rates are usually far below 10% per period, and inflation eats into real growth. Games ignore both.
Games often cap upgrades or add diminishing returns. Compounding in finance has no cap, but compounding frequency (monthly or yearly) and fees change the result.
